einzeiler: Frank Sinatra's bizarre 1979 concept album about outer space and mortality.
kurzfassung: In 1979, Frank Sinatra released Trilogy, a three-record set featuring a bizarre final disc titled The Future, composed by Gordon Jenkins. The 40-minute sci-fi concept suite took listeners on a journey through planets and existential reflections, dividing critics and fans alike. Despite being dismissed by many as a disastrous lapse in taste, the album remains a fascinating and singular oddity in Sinatra's legendary catalog.
stichpunkte: Frank Sinatra released the triple album Trilogy in 1980, featuring past, present, and future discs.
The third disc, The Future, is a 40-minute sci-fi concept suite composed by Gordon Jenkins.
Jenkins had pitched a biographical orchestral piece called The Sinatra Story to the singer as early as 1959.
Recording for The Future took place at the Shrine Auditorium with over 100 musicians performing live.
The album includes Sinatra introducing himself by his full name and singing about outer space and mortality.
Critical reception was polarized, with figures like Pete Hamill and Jonathan Schwartz condemning it as a disaster.
Radio host Jonathan Schwartz was fired after calling the record a narcissistic mess on air following a complaint from Sinatra.
Despite being widely forgotten or disliked by purists, the album found passionate defenders captivated by its sheer audacity.

clips.hook: Gordon Jenkins pitches the Sinatra story
clips.text: Composer Gordon Jenkins wrote a letter in 1959 proposing an orchestral piece about the singer's life, noting that Sinatra was among the saddest of all people.

clips.hook: Renting the Shrine Auditorium for 100 musicians
clips.text: Because no standard recording studio in Los Angeles could accommodate the massive ensemble, the production rented out a venue typically used for the Academy Awards and basketball games.

beschreibung: Welcome to the second episode of You Must Remember This, the podcast devoted to exploring the secret and or/forgotten histories of Hollywood’s first century. Today, we look back to 1979, when — while the music world was full of punk and post-disco coke rock, and the movie world was making the transition from the “New Hollywood” of the ’70s into the blockbuster age — Frank Sinatra recorded Trilogy: Past, Present and Future, a triple album with one disc each devoted to big band standards (“The Past”); covers from “the rock era” including Billy Joel and Beatles songs and also “Theme from New York, New York” (“The Present”); and, most amazingly, a 40 minute song cycle about life, love, death and visiting outer space (“The Future”). We’ll take a look at how and why “The Future” was made, and theorize as to why it’s fallen into the dustbin of pop cultural history.
